subject: religious-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: How many commandments (mitzvot) are traditionally said to be found in the Torah?
questions.explain: Jewish tradition holds that the Torah contains 613 mitzvot (commandments) to be observed.

questions.q: Which Hebrew term refers to the divine presence of God dwelling in the world?
questions.explain: Shekhinah describes the presence of God experienced as dwelling among the Jewish people.

questions.q: The covenant God made with Abraham was sealed with which sign?
questions.explain: The Abrahamic covenant was marked by circumcision (Brit Milah); the rainbow was the sign of the earlier covenant with Noah.

questions.q: At which mountain did God give the Torah and the Ten Commandments to Moses?
questions.explain: The covenant at Sinai, including the Ten Commandments, was given to Moses on Mount Sinai.

questions.q: What does the principle of 'pikuach nefesh' teach?
options: Saving a life overrides almost all other commandments
The Torah must be read every week
The Sabbath can never be broken
questions.explain: Pikuach nefesh means the preservation of human life takes precedence over nearly all other religious laws.

questions.q: What is the Hebrew term for the awaited anointed one who many Jews believe will bring an age of peace?
questions.explain: Mashiach (Messiah) means 'anointed one', a future leader expected to bring peace and restoration.

questions.q: A Jewish teaching states that after death God will reward the righteous and punish the wicked. Which characteristic of God does this express?
questions.explain: The belief that God assesses human conduct and gives what is deserved reflects God as Judge.

questions.q: What is the name of the ark in the synagogue that holds the Torah scrolls?
questions.explain: The Aron Hakodesh (Holy Ark) is the focal cupboard in which the Torah scrolls are kept.

questions.q: What is the 'Ner Tamid' in a synagogue?
questions.explain: The Ner Tamid is the continually burning light above the Ark, symbolising God's eternal presence.

questions.q: The Shema is a central Jewish prayer that above all declares:
questions.explain: The Shema affirms 'the Lord is One', a core statement of Jewish belief in one God.

questions.q: What is the name of the prayer shawl worn by many Jews during prayer?
questions.explain: The tallit is a fringed prayer shawl worn during prayer, particularly in morning services.

questions.q: What are tefillin?
options: Small leather boxes containing scripture, bound to the arm and head
Candlesticks lit at the start of Shabbat
Loaves of bread eaten on Shabbat
A scroll fixed to a doorpost
questions.explain: Tefillin are leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on the arm and head during weekday prayer; the doorpost scroll is a mezuzah.

questions.q: When does Shabbat begin and end?
questions.explain: Shabbat runs from sunset on Friday until the appearance of three stars (nightfall) on Saturday.

questions.q: What is the name for the body of Jewish laws about which foods may or may not be eaten?
questions.explain: Kashrut is the set of dietary laws determining which foods are kosher (permitted).

questions.q: A Jewish person refuses to eat a cheeseburger, explaining that meat and dairy must not be combined. Which practice are they following?
questions.explain: Keeping meat and milk separate is part of the kosher dietary laws (kashrut).

questions.q: On Friday evening a family lights two candles, blesses a cup of wine and eats plaited challah bread. Which observance is this?
questions.explain: Candles, wine (Kiddush) and challah loaves mark the welcoming of Shabbat on Friday evening.

questions.q: Which festival is the Jewish New Year, marked by the blowing of the shofar?
questions.explain: Rosh Hashanah is the Jewish New Year, when the shofar (ram's horn) is sounded.

questions.q: Yom Kippur is best described as:
options: The Day of Atonement, marked by fasting and repentance
A harvest festival celebrated in booths
The festival of the Exodus from Egypt
questions.explain: Yom Kippur is the most solemn day, a fast day devoted to repentance and seeking God's forgiveness.

questions.q: The festival of Pesach (Passover) commemorates which event?
options: The Exodus of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt
The giving of the Torah at Sinai
questions.explain: Pesach recalls the Israelites' liberation from slavery in Egypt as told in the Exodus.

questions.q: At the Pesach Seder, matzah (unleavened bread) is eaten to remind Jews that:
options: The Israelites left Egypt in haste, with no time for bread to rise
The Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed
God created the world in six days
The covenant was made with Abraham
questions.explain: Matzah recalls the hurried Exodus, when there was no time to let bread dough rise.

questions.q: At what age does a Jewish boy traditionally become Bar Mitzvah?
questions.explain: A boy becomes Bar Mitzvah ('son of the commandment') at 13, taking on adult religious responsibilities.

questions.q: A Jewish family holds a ceremony to circumcise their baby son when he is eight days old. Which rite of passage is this?
questions.explain: Brit Milah is the circumcision of a baby boy on the eighth day, marking entry into the covenant.
